title: Don't sniff the antler
translation: Don't hold young deer antler up to your nose and sniff it. They say there are tiny insects in it that crawl in through your nose and eat your brain.
original: {鹿茸|ろくじよう}を{鼻|はな}にあてて{嗅|か}ぐべからず、ちひさき{虫|むし}ありて、{鼻|はな}より{入|い}りて{脳|なう}をはむといへり。
literal: One must not put deer velvet to one's nose and smell it: they say there are small insects, which go in through the nose and eat the brain.

notes.text: {鹿茸|ろくじよう}: the young antler of a deer, still soft and covered in 'velvet'. It was a costly medicine in Chinese tradition. The 1925 edition gives the reading ろくじよう (written with a small ょ in the edition).
べからず: 'must not', the negative of べし. The same form is still used on signs today, as in {入|はい}るべからず 'keep out'.
はむ: 'to eat', written {食|は}む. The word survives in modern Japanese in {草|くさ}を{食|は}む, 'to graze'.
'They say.' いへり is いふ + り, 'it has been said'. Kenkō passes the warning on without saying whether he believes it.
